description: extends, interfaces, and one method name that does many things.

screens.body:
Inheritance lets a new class reuse an existing one. class Dog extends Animal means Dog automatically gets all of Animal's fields and methods — name, age, eat() — and then adds its own, like bark().

The relationship is IS-A: a Dog IS an Animal. If the sentence 'X is a Y' sounds wrong ('a Car is a Dog'), inheritance is the wrong tool.

JavaScript has the same idea: class Dog extends Animal works in JS too. Java just enforces types around it.

screens.heading: extends: stop repeating yourself
screens.keyPoint: extends = inherit everything, then add your own.

screens.body:
Sometimes the child needs a different behavior than the parent's. Redefining a parent's method in the child is called overriding: Dog's speak() replaces Animal's speak().

Write @Override above the method. It's optional, but it makes the compiler double-check that you're actually overriding something — if you misspell the method name, it errors instead of silently creating a new method.

The signatures must match: same name, same parameters, compatible return type.

options: This method replaces the parent's version
check.question: The @Override annotation tells the compiler…

screens.heading: @Override: my version of the method

screens.body:
Inside a child class, super refers to the parent. super(...) as the first line of a constructor calls the parent's constructor — how the child's name field gets set when the parent owns it.

You can also call overridden parent methods: super.speak() runs Animal's version even inside Dog's speak(). Useful when the child wants to extend the parent's behavior, not fully replace it.

Rule: if the parent has no no-argument constructor, the child MUST call super(...) explicitly. The compiler won't guess the arguments.
screens.heading: super: phone home to the parent

screens.body:
Here's the magic trick: a variable declared as the parent type can hold any child object. Animal a = new Dog() is legal because every Dog IS an Animal.

When you call a.speak(), Java runs DOG's version — the decision is made at runtime based on the real object, not the variable's declared type. One method call, many possible behaviors: that's polymorphism.

Why care? You can write void feed(Animal a) once, and it works for Dog, Cat, Bird — whatever comes next. JavaScript does this naturally with duck typing; Java does it with declared types.

check.question: With `Animal a = new Dog();`, a.speak() runs…

code.snippet:
Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak(); // runs Dog's speak() -> "woof"

screens.heading: Polymorphism: one type, many behaviors
screens.keyPoint: The real object's method runs, not the variable type's.

screens.body:
An interface is a pure contract: a list of method signatures with no bodies. interface Flyable { void fly(); } says 'anything that claims to fly must have a fly() method.'

A class signs the contract with implements: class Bird implements Flyable. The compiler then forces Bird to write fly() — no forgetting.

The big win over extends: a class can implement MANY interfaces (Flyable, Swimmable, …) but extend only ONE class. Interfaces describe what you CAN DO; inheritance describes what you ARE.
screens.heading: Interfaces: a contract, not a parent

screens.body:
An abstract class is a halfway house: it can mix implemented methods with abstract ones (no body) that children must fill in. You can't create objects from it directly — it's an unfinished blueprint.

So when do you pick which? Use an interface when unrelated classes share an ability (Bird and Airplane both Flyable). Use an abstract class when related classes share actual code (Dog and Cat both extend Animal's eat()).

If you're unsure, start with an interface — it's the more flexible choice, and you can always refactor later.

options: Share some implemented code with children
check.question: Reach for an abstract class when you want to…

screens.heading: Abstract classes vs interfaces
screens.keyPoint: Interface = shared ability. Abstract class = shared code.

screens.body:
Sometimes you hold a parent-type reference and need the child's extras: Animal a = new Dog(). To call a.bark(), you must cast: Dog d = (Dog) a.

Casting blindly is risky — if a is actually a Cat, you get a ClassCastException at runtime. instanceof checks first: if (a instanceof Dog) is true only when a really is a Dog.

Modern habit: check with instanceof, then cast inside the if. Safe, readable, no surprises.
